title: Length Converter
context: Grade 3, the second working topic of the metric measures chapter. An adult sees a rule, multiply by a hundred, which a child can say and not understand. What is being settled is that a metre really is a hundred centimetres, so changing the unit changes how many are counted and not how long the thing is, and that a column of centimetres can reach a hundred and must hand a metre across. A child who adds the metres and the centimetres as plain numbers writes a total that has no length at all.

writeup.why: Change metres into centimetres and back, change kilometres and metres into each other, and add and subtract lengths in columns, carrying and borrowing where a column needs it, with the unit written next to every number.
writeup.look: A metre rod in ten tens across the top, a kilometre road with posts under it, a column board for adding lengths, a trek path of five days, blank boxes for missing numbers, and the number pad down the right of the canvas.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Length Converter' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many lengths have been changed or added so far. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. A metre rod 900 long and 50 tall lies across the top of the working area at x 100, y 214, drawn in ten equal tens of ten centimetre marks, each mark near-black and the tens in alternating pale colours. A kilometre road 980 long winds under it at y 290 with a wooden post at every thousand metres, each post labelled in metres. On the first phase a length in metres and centimetres sits in a deep blue tag 300 by 80 at x 100, y 380, labelled Given. Each press of the Break button breaks one metre of the rod into a hundred centimetre marks that scatter into a tray at x 100, y 480, 560 by 150, inside a vermilion ring labelled Unit fact, where 1 m = 100 cm. The centimetres of the length sit in an amber tag at x 440, y 380, 220 by 80, labelled Second, and the total lands in a green tag at x 700, y 380, 300 by 80, labelled Answer. On the second phase a length in centimetres sits in the blue tag above a row of marks, and each press of the Gather button gathers a hundred marks into one metre rod; the marks left over stay in the amber tag, labelled Left, and the last two digits of the length are ringed in amber. On the third phase the post at x 100 slides along the road a thousand metres at a time under a vermilion ring labelled Unit fact, where 1 km = 1000 m, and the child adds the extra metres in the amber tag or gathers metres back into kilometres and metres. On the fourth phase a column board 700 by 380 at x 100, y 350 has two columns, labelled metres and centimetres or kilometres and metres, with the first length on top in a deep blue row, the second length under it in an amber row, a carry mark 60 by 40 above the metres column and a green answer row at the foot. A carried amount hops into the next column with a small click, and a borrowed metre breaks into a hundred centimetres and falls into the centimetres column. A trek path of five days winds across the board at x 820, y 350, 300 by 340, each day with a morning stone and an afternoon stone labelled in kilometres. Blank boxes 110 by 60 take a missing number. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys and a clear key, for typing a number or filling a blank, with the keys m, cm and km for the unit. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Real objects keep their own natural colours, and the chapter's four roles are carried by what holds the object or the number, never by tinting the object. The measure the question gives, or the reading taken from the ruler, the balance or the jug, sits in a deep blue tag or on a deep blue plate, labelled Given. The measure the working reaches, a converted or total amount, sits in a green tag, labelled Answer. The times 100 or times 1000 step and the unit fact it comes from sit inside a vermilion ring, labelled Unit fact. The second amount of a sum or a difference, an amount carried and a part left over sit in an amber tag, labelled Second or Left. Every ruler mark, scale mark and plain edge is near-black, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of the four, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a measure is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The board shows the last length changed or added in both units, with the metre rod or the column board that did the work still beside it.

writeup.delight: On the first phase, when the Break button is pressed, a metre of the rod snaps into a hundred marks with a soft click and the marks rain gently into the tray in ten neat tens. On the fourth phase, when a total reaches a hundred centimetres, the hundred marks gather into a small rod and hop up into the metres column all at once.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet typed. On the first phase a length in metres and centimetres sits in a deep blue tag with the metre rod lying whole across the top and the answer tag empty. On the second a length in centimetres sits in the blue tag above a long row of centimetre marks, and the tag for metres and centimetres is empty. On the third a long road runs across the bench with a kilometre post standing at its start, and a length in kilometres and metres waits in the blue tag. On the fourth a column board holds two lengths one under the other with an empty answer row and an empty carry mark above the metres column. One thing moves, once: the metre rod, the first mark, the kilometre post or the first column gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any length changed with the rod and the road, the column board in either unit pair with a carry or a borrow, and the five day trek path. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on metres into centimetres, centimetres into metres, kilometres and metres, and adding and subtracting lengths in columns, each on a real thing.

source_tool.description: A metre rod lies across the top of the working area, drawn in ten equal tens with every centimetre mark in near-black. A kilometre road runs under it with a post for every thousand metres. On the first phase a length in metres, or in metres and centimetres, sits in a deep blue tag; the metres break one by one into hundreds of centimetre marks inside a vermilion ring labelled Unit fact, where 1 m = 100 cm, and the centimetres of the length are added in an amber tag, so that, for example, 9 m 12 cm is 912 cm. On the second phase a length in centimetres sits in the blue tag and is divided by a hundred: the child reads the last two digits as the centimetres and the digits before them as the metres, and the marks gather back into metre rods. On the third phase a length in kilometres, or in kilometres and metres, is changed with the post that stands for 1 km = 1000 m, and a length in metres is gathered back into kilometres and metres. On the fourth phase a column board with two columns, metres and centimetres, or kilometres and metres, takes two lengths one under the other; the child adds or subtracts the small unit first, a total of a hundred or more is carried above the metres column, and a top amount that is too small borrows a metre. A trek path of five days, each day with a morning leg and an afternoon leg, is added day by day and then over all five days in kilometres. A number pad types a number or fills a missing blank. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many lengths have been changed or added.
source_tool.art_direction: A metre rod and a long road / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets, big enough for a small finger. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Real everyday objects, drawn as recognisable flat illustrations that a child knows at a glance: a ruler, a measuring tape, a metre rod, a paper clip, a pencil, a book, a door, a ribbon, mangoes, a loaf of bread, potatoes, a bag of salt, a two pan balance with iron weights, a kitchen scale, measuring jugs, a glass, a teacup, a bucket, a bottle, a pot, a juice packet. The object is the thing the child measures, weighs or pours, and a plain bar or tank appears only as a second view the child can switch to.

Every scale is drawn with its marks evenly spaced and its zero at the edge: a ruler from 0, a metre rod in ten equal tens, a jug in equal marks, a balance with its beam level or tilted by the true difference. A reading is always taken at a mark, never between two.

Every unit is written next to its number, and a number is never written bare where a unit belongs. A unit fact is shown with both its sides, so 1 m = 100 cm is one object and one hundred centimetre marks side by side.

Converting is something the child does: a metre rod breaks into a hundred centimetre marks, a kilogram bag pours out a thousand gram dots, a litre jug empties into a thousand millilitre drops. The vermilion ring carries the times 100 or times 1000 step while it happens.
A sum or a difference is laid out in columns, units over their column, the second amount directly under the first, with a carried amount shown above the column it joins.
Anything the stage asks to be counted is at most thirty things, separated and large enough to count at a glance. Large amounts are shown as a few tens, hundreds or thousands.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a number, a mark or a reading the child is looking at, and a content colour is never used for chrome. Real objects keep their own natural colours: a mango stays yellow and a metal weight stays dark grey. The four roles of the chapter are carried by what holds the object or the number, never by tinting the object. The measure the question gives, or the reading taken from the ruler, the balance or the jug, sits in a deep blue tag or on a deep blue plate and is labelled Given. The measure the working reaches, a converted or total amount, sits in a green tag and is labelled Answer. The times 100 or times 1000 step and the unit fact it comes from, such as one metre is one hundred centimetres, sit inside a vermilion ring and are labelled Unit fact. The second amount of a sum or a difference, an amount carried and a part left over sit in an amber tag and are labelled Second or Left. Those four are the same four in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Every ruler mark, scale mark, outline and plain edge is near-black, and the stage still reads with the colour taken away because each role is named in writing first.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Break the big unit into the small one first, then count again.
voice.onNext: A new length. Say its unit before you change it.
voice.opening: A metre rod, a long road and a board for adding.
voice.onFinish: You changed the unit and kept the length the same.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Break, gather, slide and add as you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has marked every ten centimetres on a paper strip one metre long and counted the marks, and before any rule is written on the board. The tool is what lets a metre break into a hundred marks and a kilometre post slide a thousand metres, and what carries a hundred centimetres into a metre in front of the child, which a paper strip cannot do.

answer_key.rule: One metre is 100 cm, so to change metres into centimetres multiply by 100. A length in metres and centimetres is changed by changing the metres and adding the centimetres. To change centimetres into metres divide by 100: the last two digits are the centimetres and the digits before them are the metres. One kilometre is 1000 m, so to change kilometres into metres multiply by 1000 and to change metres into kilometres divide by 1000. To add or subtract lengths, write them in columns with the small unit on one side, work the small unit first, carry a hundred centimetres or a thousand metres into the next column, and borrow a metre or a kilometre when the top amount is too small. Keep the unit written next to every number.
answer_key.wrong: The metres break into their centimetre marks again beside the child's answer, the last two digits are lit in amber, and the columns are worked again one at a time with the carried or borrowed amount shown above the column it joins. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: One metre is one hundred centimetres.
Change the metres first. Six metres is six hundreds of centimetres, so six hundred centimetres.
Then add the 37 cm. Six hundred and 37 is 637.
items.question: A kite string is 6 m 37 cm long. How many centimetres is that?
items.checkpoint: Change the metres into centimetres first, then add the centimetres.
items.misconception: Adding the metres and the centimetres as plain numbers, 6 plus 37, instead of changing the metres first.

steps: A hundred centimetres make one metre, so divide by a hundred.
The last two digits of 834 are 34, so there are 34 cm.
The digits before them are 8, so there are 8 m.
items.question: A ribbon on a reel is 834 cm long. How many metres and centimetres is that?
items.checkpoint: The last two digits are the centimetres and the digits before them are the metres.
items.misconception: Taking only the last digit as the centimetres and writing 83 m 4 cm.

steps: One kilometre is a thousand metres.
Change the kilometres first. Six kilometres is six thousand metres.
Then add the 275 m. Six thousand and 275 is 6275.
items.question: A road from the village to the river is 6 km 275 m long. How many metres is that?
items.checkpoint: Change the kilometres into metres first, then add the metres.
items.misconception: Multiplying by a hundred instead of a thousand, because a hundred is the number used with centimetres.

steps: Write the lengths in two columns, metres and centimetres, one under the other.
Add the centimetres first: 74 cm + 69 cm = 143 cm.
143 cm is 1 m 43 cm. Write 43 cm and carry the 1 m to the metres column.
In the metres column, 2 and 1 and the carried 1 give 4 m.
So 2 m 74 cm + 1 m 69 cm = 4 m 43 cm.
items.question: A rope is cut in two pieces. One piece is 2 m 74 cm long and the other is 1 m 69 cm long. How long was the rope before it was cut? Add in columns.
items.checkpoint: Add the small unit first and carry into the next column when it reaches a hundred.
items.misconception: Writing 143 cm in the centimetres column and leaving the metres column at 3 m.

items.question: A shelf for school books is 3 m 29 cm long. How many centimetres is that?
items.final_answer: 329 cm, because 3 m 29 cm is three hundreds of centimetres and 29 more

A bus drives 21 km to one town and then 34 km more to the next town. How far has the bus driven in all?
A school wall is 13 m long. How many centimetres is that?
items.final_answer: 1300 cm, because 13 m is thirteen hundreds of centimetres

items.question: A train coach is 1867 cm long. How many metres and centimetres is that?
A cycle path is 7461 m long. How many kilometres and metres is that?
A tailor cuts a piece 2 m 47 cm long from a roll of cloth that is 5 m 28 cm long. How much cloth is left on the roll? Subtract in columns.
items.final_answer: 2 m 81 cm, because 5 m 28 cm is 4 m 128 cm after borrowing a metre, and 128 cm - 47 cm = 81 cm

student_controls.effect: breaks one metre at a time into a hundred centimetre marks in ten tens
slides a post along the road a thousand metres at a time
turn big units into small ones, or gather small ones back into big ones

teaching_notes: Give each pair a paper strip one metre long to mark every ten centimetres before the tool opens, and let them count the marks and say how many centimetres make a metre. Insist that the metres are changed first and the centimetres added after, and that the unit is written next to every number. Say that the last two digits of a length in centimetres are the centimetres. Use a real road, a rope or a ribbon for each question, never a bare number. If a child adds metres and centimetres as plain numbers, ask which unit the answer would be in. If a child leaves a hundred or more in the centimetres column, ask how many metres a hundred centimetres make. Use fresh numbers: the exercise's lengths are the child's to convert.
generation_prompt: Build a length conversion tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage, drawn as flat illustrations of real things in natural colours. A metre rod lies across the top of the working area, drawn in ten equal tens with every centimetre mark in near-black, and a kilometre road runs under it with a post for every thousand metres. A length sits in a deep blue tag. On the first phase each metre breaks into a hundred centimetre marks inside a vermilion ring labelled Unit fact and the centimetres are added in an amber tag; on the second phase the marks gather back into metre rods and the last two digits are read as the centimetres; on the third phase a post slides along the road a thousand metres at a time. On the fourth phase a column board with a metres column and a centimetres column, or a kilometres column and a metres column, takes two lengths one under the other, with a carry mark above the metres column and a borrow mark that moves a metre down, and a trek path of five days with a morning leg and an afternoon leg is added in kilometres. Blank boxes take a missing number. The answer lands in a green tag. The number pad types a number or fills a blank. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the lengths changed or added. No people, hands or faces. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Break the metres into centimetres. Gather the centimetres back into metres. Slide the post along the road. Add and subtract lengths in columns, small unit first.
